about: The Milky Way for Seebra's 3D example: the spiral arms as Reid et al. (2019) fitted them to maser parallaxes, the published scales of the bar, bulge and disc, real objects at measured distances, and the outer solar system out to the nearest stars. Every number carries its source; drawing choices (particle counts, colours, how far an arm is carried past its measurements) are marked as such.

galaxy.R0_source: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, A&A 625, L10: 8178 ± 13 (stat) ± 22 (sys) pc, from the orbit of the star S2 around Sgr A*
galaxy.z_sun_source: Bennett & Bovy 2019, MNRAS 482, 1417: 20.8 ± 0.3 pc above the mid-plane
galaxy.bar_source: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529 and Wegg, Gerhard & Portail 2015, MNRAS 450, 4050: long bar half-length 5.0 ± 0.2 kpc at 28–33° to the Sun–centre line; the boxy/peanut bulge at 27 ± 2°. Drawn at 30°, near end at positive longitude
galaxy.disc_source: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016: thin disc scale length 2.6 ± 0.5 kpc, scale height 300 ± 50 pc; thick disc scale height 900 ± 180 pc
galaxy.arm_shape_source: Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131: ln(R/R_kink) = −(β − β_kink) tan ψ, β = 0 toward the Sun and growing with Galactic rotation; widths grow as w(R) = 336 + 36 (R − 8.15) pc; vertical scatter 20 + 36 (R − 7) pc beyond 7 kpc
galaxy.extrapolate_note: Drawing choice: each arm is carried on up to 120° beyond Reid's measured azimuths (dashed), while it stays between 2.6 and 16 kpc from the centre. The far side of the Galaxy has few maser parallaxes, so this part is a guess.

arms.name: 3-kpc
arms.note: the near 3-kpc arm, at the bar's end

arms.name: Norma
arms.note: continues as the Outer arm on the far side

arms.name: Scutum–Centaurus
arms.note: one of the two major arms

arms.name: Sagittarius–Carina
arms.note: the arm inside the Sun's orbit

arms.name: Local (Orion Spur)
arms.note: the Sun's own arm, a spur or a short arm

arms.name: Perseus
arms.note: the other major arm, outside the Sun's orbit

arms.name: Outer
arms.note: the outer end of the Norma arm

arms_source: Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131, Table 2 (β_kink without uncertainty were assigned, not fitted)

objects.name: Sgr A*
objects.method: orbit of the star S2 (GRAVITY interferometry)
objects.source: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, A&A 625, L10; mass: 2021, A&A 647, A59

objects.name: Orion Nebula
objects.method: VLBA trigonometric parallax of radio stars in the cluster

objects.name: Pleiades
objects.fact: Hipparcos had said 120.2 ± 1.5 pc: a famous disagreement that VLBI and Gaia settled

objects.name: Hyades
objects.fact: the nearest open cluster (Röser et al. 2019 give 47.50 ± 0.15 pc)

objects.name: Carina Nebula
objects.method: expansion of Eta Carinae's Homunculus nebula
objects.fact: home of Eta Carinae, one of the most massive stars known

objects.name: Eagle Nebula
objects.method: Gaia DR2 parallaxes of NGC 6611's stars

objects.name: Crab Nebula
objects.method: VLBI parallax of the Crab pulsar (+0.22/−0.18 kpc)
objects.fact: the remnant of the supernova seen in 1054
objects.source: Lin et al. 2023, ApJ (VLBA parallax 0.53 ± 0.06 mas); older estimate 2.0 kpc (Trimble 1973)

objects.name: Omega Centauri
objects.method: Gaia EDR3 parallaxes combined with other distances
objects.fact: the Milky Way's largest globular cluster, perhaps a captured galaxy's core

objects.name: Cygnus X-1
objects.fact: the first black hole found (21 solar masses)

objects.name: Westerlund 1
objects.method: Gaia parallax with an eclipsing binary
objects.fact: the most massive young cluster known in the Galaxy

objects_note: Galactic coordinates (l, b) from SIMBAD, to about 0.01°.

solar.planets_source: JPL, approximate positions of the planets (Standish), semi-major axes at J2000

belts.name: Main asteroid belt
belts.source: Kirkwood gaps at the 4:1 and 2:1 resonances with Jupiter (JPL)

belts.name: Kuiper belt
belts.note: the classical belt is about 42–48 AU; Pluto, Arrokoth
belts.source: NASA Science, Kuiper Belt facts; classification: Gladman, Marsden & VanLaerhoven 2008

belts.name: Scattered disc
belts.note: rough range: perihelia beyond about 30 AU, aphelia out to about 1,000 AU; Eris
belts.source: Gladman et al. 2008 (The Solar System Beyond Neptune, p. 43); edges approximate

belts.name: Inner (Hills) Oort cloud
belts.note: HYPOTHESISED: inferred from long-period comets and Sedna-like orbits, never observed. NASA puts the inner edge at 2,000–5,000 AU; Duncan, Quinn & Tremaine (1987) at about 3,000 AU
belts.source: Hills 1981, AJ 86, 1730; NASA Science, Oort Cloud facts; Dones et al. 2004 (Comets II, p. 153)

belts.name: Outer Oort cloud
belts.note: HYPOTHESISED: proposed by Oort (1950) from where long-period comets come from; no Oort cloud body has been seen there. The outer edge is put at 10,000–100,000 AU (NASA) or about 200,000 AU (Duncan et al. 1987)
belts.source: Oort 1950, BAN 11, 91; NASA Science, Oort Cloud facts

heliosphere.note: crossed by Voyager 1 at 94 and 121.6 AU, Voyager 2 at 83.7 and 119.0 AU; its shape away from the Voyagers' directions is not measured

voyagers.name: Voyager 1
voyagers.source: position: Heavens-Above Solar escape, 18 Nov 2026; crossings: Stone et al. 2005 (Science 309, 2017), Stone et al. 2013 (Science 341, 150)

voyagers.name: Voyager 2
voyagers.source: position: Heavens-Above Solar escape, 18 Nov 2026; crossings: Stone et al. 2008 (Nature 454, 71), Stone et al. 2019 (Nature Astronomy 3, 1013)

comets.name: C/1996 B2 (Hyakutake)
comets.fact: passed 0.1 AU from Earth in March 1996

comets.name: C/2006 P1 (McNaught)
comets.kind: comet on a hyperbolic osculating orbit
comets.fact: e ≥ 1 at this epoch: no aphelion, leaving the planets' region for good

comets.name: 90377 Sedna
comets.kind: detached object, perhaps from the inner Oort cloud
comets.fact: never comes closer than 76 AU: Neptune can't have put it there

solar.comets_note: Heliocentric osculating elements from JPL's Small-Body Database at the epoch given, rounded to three significant figures (e from q and a). The barycentric 'original' orbits of long-period comets differ, and so do their aphelia.

stars.name: Proxima Centauri
stars.fact: the nearest star to the Sun; parallax 768.067 ± 0.050 mas; host of the planet Proxima b
stars.source: Gaia DR3 (Gaia Collaboration, Vallenari et al. 2023, A&A 674, A1)

stars.name: Barnard's Star
stars.fact: the fastest-moving star on our sky; parallax 546.976 ± 0.040 mas
stars.source: Gaia DR3 (Gaia Collaboration, Vallenari et al. 2023, A&A 674, A1)
